lesson.title: When the Reading Frame Slips: Frameshift Mutations
lesson.summary: Frameshift mutations insert or delete a number of nucleotides that is not a multiple of three, which shifts the triplet reading frame for every codon downstream of the change and usually scrambles the resulting protein.
lesson.body:
A point mutation changes one codon and leaves the rest of the message intact, but insertions and deletions behave very differently. The ribosome reads an mRNA strictly three nucleotides at a time, starting from a fixed point, with no punctuation between codons. If a mutation inserts or deletes a number of bases that is a multiple of three, the reading frame downstream is preserved: one or more codons are simply added or removed, and the rest of the protein is usually unaffected. But if the number of bases inserted or deleted is not a multiple of three, every codon from that point forward is regrouped incorrectly. This is a frameshift mutation, and it is typically far more disruptive than a single point mutation.

An example makes the effect clear. Suppose a short stretch of mRNA reads AUG GCU AAU CGU UAA, which the ribosome translates as methionine, alanine, asparagine, arginine, then stop. Now delete a single nucleotide, the G at the start of the second codon. The remaining bases do not simply lose one codon; they are read three at a time starting from the very same point as before, so the sequence regroups as AUG CUA AUC GUU AA. The first codon is unchanged, still methionine, but every codon after it is new: leucine, isoleucine, valine, and so on, none of which match the original protein. Worse, the original UAA stop codon has been destroyed by the shift, so the ribosome keeps translating into sequence that was never meant to be read as protein, until it happens to encounter a new stop codon, by chance, somewhere further along. The result is usually a protein with a completely wrong amino acid sequence from the mutation site onward, often cut short or extended at an unpredictable length, and rarely functional.

Frameshift mutations do not only arise from mutagen damage or a simple replication error; they are especially associated with a phenomenon called slipped strand mispairing, in which the template or the newly made strand transiently loops out during replication, particularly in stretches of DNA that contain short repeated sequences, where the strands can misalign and still base pair correctly a few bases off from where they should. Because the lagging strand is synthesized discontinuously, in short Okazaki fragments that each require the polymerase to stop, release, and reinitiate synthesis nearby, it offers more opportunities for this kind of misalignment than the continuously synthesized leading strand. A loop out in the template strand leads to a deletion in the new strand, and a loop out in the new strand leads to an insertion, and either one, if not a multiple of three bases and not corrected by proofreading, becomes a frameshift.

The general lesson carries forward through the rest of this unit: the size of a mutation does not predict its severity nearly as well as whether it preserves the reading frame. A single substituted base changes at most one amino acid. A single inserted or deleted base, despite looking like an even smaller change on paper, can rewrite an entire protein from that point on.
